title: The Village That Hid Refugees
text:
Le Chambon-sur-Lignon is a village on a high, cold plateau in south-central France, home to a Protestant community descended from the persecuted Huguenots. When France fell in 1940, its pastor, Andre Trocme, and his assistant Edouard Theis preached that Christians must resist evil, but only with what they called the weapons of the spirit.

During the war the village and the surrounding plateau sheltered refugees, many of them Jewish children whose parents had been deported. They were hidden in homes, farms, boarding houses and schools. Villagers forged identity papers and ration cards, and some guided refugees across the mountains to Switzerland. Magda Trocme, the pastor's wife, opened her door to anyone who knocked. In his study of the village, the philosopher Philip Hallie wrote that she said the first refugee simply needed to come in, and she did not think further than that.

In 1942 a Vichy minister visited and was handed a letter from the village's youth saying they would hide Jews no matter what. When officials demanded a list of the Jews in the village, Trocme refused. In 1943 he and Theis were arrested and held for several weeks. Trocme's cousin Daniel, who ran a children's home there, was later deported and died at Majdanek.

The plateau is credited with saving thousands of people. In 1990 Yad Vashem honored the community as a whole as Righteous Among the Nations.
lesson: Shared values make individual courage easier. When a whole community quietly agrees on what is right, each person's risky act feels less alone.
people: Andre and Magda Trocme, Edouard Theis, Daniel Trocme, villagers of the plateau
source: Philip Hallie, Lest Innocent Blood Be Shed (1979); Yad Vashem, Righteous Among the Nations records
caveat: Estimates of the number of people sheltered vary widely, from about 3,000 to 5,000.
